newsitem.title: GERMANY: Broad Thyssen-Krupp link could help both - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Broad Thyssen-Krupp link could help both - analysts.

text.p: A merger between German industrial groups Thyssen AG and Krupp, now negotiating a marriage of their flat steel operations, would help them face global challenges, equities analysts said on Monday.
Such a fusion would create Germany's fifth largest industrial company with about 65 billion marks in sales in capital goods, plant construction and related services as well as steel.
Speculation over a full merger has revived after reports that the two would soon announce details of their steel tie-up.

Weekly news magazine Der Spiegel said senior management at Thyssen and Fried. Krupp AG Hoesch-Krupp have met for talks to discuss a merger of the two groups once the deal to combine their flat steel units is approved in coming weeks.
The Berliner Zeitung reported that the companies would announce details of their planned steel merger on September 3 and begin talks on broader cooperation immediately.
The twist this time is that not Krupp but Thyssen, with its deeper pockets, appears to be calling the shots.

As Krupp chairman Gerhard Cromme showed in March with a brash hostile takeover bid for larger rival Thyssen -- a move virtually unheard of in Germany -- Krupp's style is quicker and more aggressive, while Thyssen is more cautious and deliberate.
Concerted protests by workers and political leaders forced Cromme to retreat from his initial bid and compromise on the steel plan. But the prospect of building a mega-company still has its fans.
"It makes a lot of sense for them to be together. If you merged both cultures, you'd be really there," said analyst Alan Coats with Merrill Lynch in London.
"Stainless and steel have been sorted out. The question now is how to make themselves more of a world force in the rest of the business. The business is going global," Coats said.

Der Spiegel said that with Thyssen in command, the new entity would not be saddled with the nine billion marks in debt Cromme planned to borrow to pay for the deal and it would not have to chop profitable operations.

"That's a total change in attitude," said analyst Peter Fish at Britain's MEPS steel research institute. "The steel merger is going faster than initially expected. People saw lots of problems but the latest talk is that it's all coming together now."

Thyssen spokesman Reiner Hochscheid said the planned steel merger would address 75 percent of the potential synergy effects between the two companies and that the two might then see what they could do about the remaining 25 percent.
A complete merger would be "a theoretically conceivable possibility" but it would require long and detailed negotiations, Hochscheid said.
The two companies already indicated last spring that trade and automobile parts were two further potential areas for cooperation, he said.
No comment was available from Krupp.
Analyst Richard Schramm at Trinkaus & Burkhardt in Duesseldorf said the more fields the companies cooperated in, the more sense it made for them to merge completely.
While Krupp originally sought to take over Thyssen to deal with its own strategic difficulties, the move would have saddled it with huge debts.

Krupp still has to bear the costs of the steel merger and come up with several million marks in cash to bring its equity share in the steel venture up to 40 percent as agreed. And it must guarantee Thyssen a profit of 300 million marks a year.
Thyssen, meanwhile, has been calmly going about an international diversification plan, acquiring U.S. machine tool maker Giddings & Lewis and metals trade Copper & Brass Sales.

A broader merger could yield cost savings and would not necessarily entail deeper personnel cuts, Coats said, adding: "Krupp already has lots of pension liabilities from past downsizing. There's not that much to go and the issues have been well stated."
-- Bonn newsroom, 49-228-26097150
